# Variational inference {#sec-variationalinference}

## Generative modeling

The input data $X = \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N$ comes from an unknown distribution of pdf $p(x)$. The training set $\mathcal{D}$ is formed by **samples** of that distribution. Learning the distribution of the data means learning a **parameterized distribution** $p_\theta(x)$ that is as close as possible to the true distribution $p(x)$.

The parameterized distribution could be a family of known distributions (e.g. normal) or a neural network with a softmax output layer.

This means that we want to minimize the KL between the two distributions:

$$
    \min_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x)) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [- \log \dfrac{p_\theta(x)}{p(x)}]
$$

The problem is that we do not know $p(x)$ as it is what we want to learn, so we cannot estimate the KL directly. When trying to learn the distribution $p(x)$ of the data directly, we could use the same trick as in maximum likelihood estimation (@sec-klml):

$$
    \nabla_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x)) = \nabla_\theta \, H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) = \nabla_\theta \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [- \log p_\theta(x)]
$$

i.e. maximize the log-likelihood of the model on the data $\mathcal{D}$.

If we use $N$ data samples to estimate the expectation, we notice that:

$$
    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [\log p_\theta(x)] \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(x_i) = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \log \prod_{i=1}^N p_\theta(x_i) = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \log L(\theta)
$$

is indeed the log-likelihood of the model on the data that we maximize in **maximum likelihood estimation** (@sec-mle).

The problem is that images are **high-dimensional** (one dimension per pixel), so we would need astronomical numbers of samples to estimate the gradient (once): this is the **curse of dimensionality**.

![The curse of dimensionality. Source: <https://dibyaghosh.com/blog/probability/highdimensionalgeometry.html>](img/curse-of-dimensionality.png){#fig-cursedimensionality width=70%}

MLE does not work well in high-dimensional spaces. We need to work in a much lower-dimensional space.

Images are not random samples of the pixel space: **natural images** are embedded in a much lower-dimensional space called a **manifold**. A manifold is a **locally Euclidean** topological space of lower dimension. The surface of the earth is locally flat and 2D, but globally spherical and 3D.

> If we have a **generative model** $p(x | z)$ telling us how a sample $z$ on the manifold maps to the image space, we would only need to learn the distribution of the data in the lower-dimensional **latent space**.

The low-dimensional **latent variables** $z$ are the actual cause for the observations $x$. Given a sample $z$ on the manifold, we can train a **generative model** $p_\theta(x | z)$ to recreate the input $x$. $p_\theta(x | z)$ is the **decoder**: given a latent representation $z$, what is the corresponding observation $x$?

![Latent variable model. Source: <https://blog.evjang.com/2016/08/variational-bayes.html>](img/latent-variable-model.png){#fig-latentvariable width=50%}

If we learn the distribution $p_\theta(z)$ of the manifold (latent space), we can infer the distribution of the data $p_\theta(x)$ using that model (**marginalization**):

$$
    p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_\theta(z)} [p_\theta(x | z)] = \int_z p_\theta(x | z) \, p_\theta(z) \, dz
$$

Problem: we do not know $p_\theta(z)$, as the only data we see is $x$: $z$ is called a **latent variable** because it explains the data but is hidden.

## Variational inference: first explanation

To estimate $p_\theta(z)$, we could again marginalize over $x$:

$$
    p_\theta(z) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\theta(x)} [p_\theta(z | x)] = \int_x p_\theta(z | x) \, p_\theta(x) \, dx
$$

$p_\theta(z | x)$ is the **encoder**: given an input $x \sim p_\theta(x)$, what is its latent representation $z$?

The Bayes rule tells us:

$$
    p_\theta(z | x) = p_\theta(x |z) \, \dfrac{p_\theta(z)}{p_\theta(x)}
$$

The **posterior** probability (encoder) $p_\theta(z | x)$ depends on the **model** (decoder) $p_\theta(x|z)$, the **prior** (assumption) $p_\theta(z)$ and the **evidence** (data) $p_\theta(x)$.

The posterior is **intractable**, as the evidence $p_\theta(x) = \int_z p_\theta(x | z) \, p_\theta(z) \, dz$ would require to integrate over all possible latent representations $z$.

**Variational inference** proposes to approximate the true posterior (encoder) $p_\theta(z | x)$ by another parameterized distribution $q_\phi(z|x)$.

![Graphical model of a VAE. Source: <https://lilianweng.github.io/lil-log/2018/08/12/from-autoencoder-to-beta-vae.html>](img/vae-graphical-model.png){#fig-vaegraphicalmodel width=70%}

The decoder $p_\theta(x |z)$ generates observations $x$ from a latent representation $z$ with parameters $\theta$. The encoder $q_\phi(z|x)$ estimates the latent representation $z$ of a generated observation $x$. It should approximate $p_\theta(z | x)$ with parameters $\phi$.

To make $q_\phi(z| x)$ close to $p_\theta(z | x)$, we minimize their KL divergence:

$$
    \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) ) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log \dfrac{p_\theta(z | x)}{q_\phi(z|x)}]
$$

Note that we sample the latent representations from the learned encoder $q_\phi(z|x)$ (imagination). As $p_\theta(z | x) = p_\theta(x |z) \, \dfrac{p_\theta(z)}{p_\theta(x)}$, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) ) &= \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log \dfrac{p_\theta(x | z) \, p_\theta(z)}{q_\phi(z|x) \, p_\theta(x)}]\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log \dfrac{p_\theta(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}] - \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x | z)]\\
\end{aligned}
$$

$p_\theta(x)$ does not depend on $z$, so its expectation w.r.t $z$ is constant:

$$
    \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) ) = \text{KL}(q_\phi(z| x) || p_\theta(z)) + \log p_\theta(x) + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x | z)]
$$

We rearrange the terms:

$$
    \log p_\theta(x) - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) ) = - \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x | z)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z))
$$

* Training the **encoder** means that we **minimize** $\text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) )$, i.e. we want the encoder $q_\phi(z | x)$ to be close to the true "inverse" of the decoder.
* Training the **decoder** means that we **maximize** $\log p_\theta(x)$ (log-likelihood of the model), i.e. we generate realistic data / explain the data samples.
* Training the encoder and decoder together means that we **maximize**:

$$
    \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) = \log p_\theta(x) - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) )
$$

The KL divergence is always positive or equal to 0, so we have:

$$
    \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) \leq \log p_\theta(x)
$$

This term is called the **evidence lower bound** (ELBO): by maximizing it, we also maximize the intractable evidence $\log p_\theta(x)$, which is what we want to do (see the second explanation for the reason).

The trick is that the right-hand term of the equation gives us a tractable definition of the ELBO term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) &= \log p_\theta(x) - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z | x) ) \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [\log p_\theta(x | z)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z))
\end{aligned}
$$

What happens when we **minimize** the negative ELBO?

$$
    \mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) = - \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x | z)] + \text{KL}(q_\phi(z| x) || p_\theta(z))
$$

* $\mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [- \log p_\theta(x | z)]$ is the **reconstruction loss** of the decoder $p_\theta(x | z)$: given a sample $z$ of the encoder $q_\phi(z|x)$, minimize the negative log-likelihood of the reconstruction $p_\theta(x | z)$.

* $\text{KL}(q_\phi(z| x) || p_\theta(z))$ is the **regularization loss** for the encoder: the latent distribution $q_\phi(z|x)$ should not be too far from the **prior** $p_\theta(z)$.

## Variational inference: second explanation

A very satisfying explanation can be found in @Luo2022a.

Our goal is to maximize the log-likelihood of the generative model on the samples $x$, conditioned on the latent variable $z$:

$$
    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [\log p_\theta(x)]  = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [\log \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)} [p_\theta(x | z)]]
$$

To get the model (decoder) $p_\theta(x | z)$, we could use the Bayes rule, but the true posterior $p_\theta(z | x)$ is intractable:

$$
    p_\theta(z | x) = p_\theta(x |z) \, \dfrac{p_\theta(z)}{p_\theta(x)}
$$

because we would need to normalize with $p_\theta(x)$, the unknown evidence.

We therefore want to approximate it using the approximate posterior $q_\phi(z | x) \approx p_\theta(z | x)$ (@fig-vaegraphicalmodel).

A first way to obtain the ELBO is using importance sampling and Jensen's inequality ($f(\mathbb{E}[X]) \geq \mathbb{E}[f(X)]$ if $f$ is concave, like the logarithm):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(x) &= \log \int p_\theta(x, z) \, dz & \text{(Marginalize over } z) \\
& = \log \int  q_\phi(z|x) \, \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \, dz & \text{(Introduce the encoder)}\\
& = \log \mathbb{E}_{z \sim  q_\phi(z|x)} [\dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}] & \text{(Get an expectation)}\\
& \geq \mathbb{E}_{z \sim  q_\phi(z|x)} [\log \, \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}] & \text{(Jensen's inequality)}\\
& = \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) &\\
\end{aligned}
$$

People usually stop there and say that maximizing the ELBO also maximizes the log-likelihood, but there is no reason for this to be true unless the difference between the log-likelihood and the ELBO is also **minimized**.

So let's decompose the log-likelihood (evidence) fully:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \log p_\theta(x) & = \log p_\theta(x) \, \int q_\phi(z | x) \, dz& \text{(The integral is one by definition)} \\
     & =  \int q_\phi(z | x) \log p_\theta(x) \, dz& \text{(We can move the evidence inside)} \\
     & =  \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [\log p_\theta(x) ] & \text{(It becomes an expectation)} \\
     & =  \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [\log \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{p_\theta(z|x)} ] & \text{(Definition of conditional)} \\
     & =  \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [\log \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z) \, q_\phi(z|x)}{p_\theta(z|x) \, q_\phi(z|x)} ] & \text{(Introduce the encoder)} \\
     & =  \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [\log \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} ] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [ - \log \dfrac{p_\theta(z|x)}{q_\phi(z|x)} ] & \text{(Split the expectation)} \\
     & =  \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) + \text{KL}( q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z|x)) &  \\
\end{aligned}
$$

Alright, so the difference between the evidence and the ELBO is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the **true posterior** $p_\theta(z|x)$ and the approximate posterior $q_\phi(z|x)$, i.e. how well the encoder models the latent space.

So how does maximizing the ELBO lead to maximizing the log-likelihood $\log \, p_\theta(x)$? The trick is that $\log \, p_\theta(x)$ **does not depend on** $\phi$, the parameters of the encoder. Said otherwise, $\log \, p_\theta(x)$ is a constant with respect to $\phi$ and its gradient is zero:

$$
    \underbrace{\nabla_\phi \, \log \, p_\theta(x)}_{ = 0} = \underbrace{\nabla_\phi \, \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi)}_{\text{maximized}} + \underbrace{\nabla_\phi \,  \text{KL}( q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z|x))}_{\text{minimized}}
$$

As the sum of both terms must be equal to 0, **maximizing the ELBO also minimizes the KL between the true posterior and the approximate posterior!** The evidence is therefore also maximized, as the difference between the evidence and the ELBO is minimized...

Intuitively, this means that in order to get a good reconstruction from the latent representation, you need a good latent representation...

The tractable definition of the ELBO is minus the KL between the encoder $q_\phi(z | x)$ and the joint $p_\theta(x, z)$, which can be split into a reconstruction term (decoder) and a regularization term on the latent using a prior $p_\theta(z)$:

$$
    \max_{\theta, \phi} \, \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z | x)} [\log \dfrac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} ] = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} [\log p_\theta(x | z)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p_\theta(z))
$$

## Variational autoencoders {#sec-vae}

**Variational autoencoders** [@Kingma2013] use $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ as a prior for the latent space, but any other prior could be used in principle. The VAE loss is the opposite of the ELBO:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\theta, \phi} \, \mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) &= \mathcal{L}_\text{reconstruction}(\theta, \phi) + \mathcal{L}_\text{regularization}(\phi) \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{z} \sim q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})} [ - \log p_\theta(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z})] + \text{KL}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) || \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}))\\
\end{aligned}
$$

The reparameterization trick and the fact that the KL between normal distributions has a closed form allow us to use backpropagation end-to-end.

The advantage of minimizing the KL of $q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})$ with $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ is that the KL takes a **closed form** when the distributions are normal (@sec-klnormal), i.e. there is no need to compute the expectation over all possible latent representations $\mathbf{z}$:

$$
    \mathcal{L}_\text{regularization}(\phi) = \text{KL}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) || \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1})) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{z} \sim q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}[- \log \frac{f_{0, 1}(\mathbf{z})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}]
$$

If $\mathbf{\mu_x}$ and $\mathbf{\sigma_x}$ have $K$ elements (dimension of the latent space), the KL can be expressed as:

$$
    \mathcal{L}_\text{regularization}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}}[\dfrac{1}{2} \, \sum_{k=1}^K (\mathbf{\sigma_x^2} + \mathbf{\mu_x}^2 -1 - \log \mathbf{\sigma_x^2})]
$$

The KL is very easy to differentiate w.r.t $\mathbf{\mu_x}$ and $\mathbf{\sigma_x}$, i.e. w.r.t $\phi$! In practice, the encoder predicts the vectors $\mathbf{\mu_x}$ and $\Sigma_\mathbf{x} = \log \mathbf{\sigma_x^2}$, so the loss becomes:

$$
    \mathcal{L}_\text{regularization}(\phi) = \dfrac{1}{2} \, \sum_{k=1}^K (\exp \Sigma_\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\mu_x}^2 -1 - \Sigma_\mathbf{x})
$$

The encoder $q_\phi(z|x)$ and decoder $p_\theta(x | z)$ are neural networks in a VAE, but other parameterized distributions can be used (e.g. in physics).

![Variational autoencoder with the reparameterization trick. Source: <https://ijdykeman.github.io/ml/2016/12/21/cvae.html>](img/vae-reparameterization.png){#fig-vaereparameterization width=70%}
